title: Email + Password Authentication
learningObjectives: Identify the right clarifying questions before designing an auth system
Design a secure credential storage model (hashing, separate tables)
Think through failure modes: brute force, enumeration, timing attacks
Evaluate trade-offs between session and token-based auth
keyTradeoffs: Sessions (server-side, revocable) vs JWT (stateless, can't revoke easily)
commonPitfalls: Storing passwords in plain text or with weak hashing (MD5, SHA-1)
Revealing whether email or password was wrong in error messages
No rate limiting on login attempts
Forgetting to hash session tokens before storing them
transferPrompt: Now design a Password Reset flow. What questions would you ask first? How does the data model change? What are the abuse risks?

1.coachQuestion: Before writing any code for email + password authentication, what questions would you ask to clarify the requirements?

junior.point: Who are the users (end users, admins, or both)?
What scale are we expecting (hundreds, thousands, millions)?
Is email the only login method, or will social login come later?
Must emails be verified before the user can access the app?
Are there password policy constraints (minimum length, checking breach lists)?

mid.point: Multi-device support — can users be logged in on phone and laptop simultaneously?
Session limits — max concurrent sessions per user?
Remember-me functionality and session duration policies needed?
Email branding requirements (custom domain, transactional email provider)?

senior.point: SSO integration path (SAML, OIDC) for future enterprise use?
Account linking — what if they sign up with email then want to add Google?
Audit log requirements for compliance (SOC2, HIPAA)?
Regulatory jurisdiction differences in password policies and data residency?
Data residency constraints (EU GDPR storage restrictions)?

modelAnswer.junior: Before writing any code, I'd ask: Who uses this — just end users or also admins? How many users — hundreds or millions? Is email the only login or will we add Google/GitHub later? Must users verify their email before they can do anything? Are there specific password policies we must follow? The answers change the entire design — admin access needs RBAC, scale affects session storage choice, and social login means the credential model needs to be extensible.
modelAnswer.mid: In addition to the basics (who, scale, email-only vs social): I'd ask about multi-device behavior — can users be logged in on phone and laptop simultaneously? Do we need 'remember me' with extended session duration? Should login/verification emails be branded (custom domain, templates)? These affect session architecture and email service requirements.
modelAnswer.senior: Beyond the standard questions: I'd clarify the SSO integration path — if the company uses Okta or Azure AD, we may need SAML/OIDC support later, which changes the credential model. I'd ask about account linking (email signup → later add Google login), audit log requirements for SOC2/HIPAA, data residency constraints, and which jurisdictions' password policies apply (NIST vs OWASP vs local regulations).

5.coachQuestion: Design the data model for email + password authentication. What tables do you need, what columns, and what constraints?

junior.point: users table: id (PK), email (UNIQUE, NOT NULL), created_at, updated_at
Separate credentials table (password_hash, foreign key to user, NOT in the users table)
Never store plain-text passwords — use salted argon2id or bcrypt
sessions table: id/token (hashed before storage), user_id (FK), expires_at, created_at
Indexes on email (login lookup) and session_token (validation on every request)

mid.point: email_verified timestamp on users (recording when verified)
failed_login_attempts counter + locked_until timestamp for progressive lockout
password_changed_at for session invalidation and audit tracking
IP address and user_agent on sessions for security review / anomaly detection
Soft-delete consideration (deleted_at vs hard delete for recovery)

senior.point: credential_history table for password reuse prevention (last N hashes)
audit_log table for login/logout/failed attempt security events
account_links table for future social login (provider, provider_id, user_id)
Sharding strategy for users table at scale (user_id partition key)
GDPR right-to-delete design (anonymizing user record vs hard-deleting credentials)

modelAnswer.junior: I'd separate concerns into three tables: A `users` table for identity (id, email with UNIQUE constraint, created_at, updated_at). A `credentials` table for the password hash — never store plain-text passwords, use argon2id or bcrypt. I keep credentials separate because you might add social login later, and not every user will have a password. A `sessions` table holds the session token (hashed, not plain), user_id FK, expires_at, and created_at. Key indexes: email for login lookup, session_token for validation on every request.
modelAnswer.mid: Building on the basics: I'd add `email_verified` (timestamp, not just boolean — you want to know when), `failed_login_attempts` counter with `locked_until` timestamp for progressive lockout, and `password_changed_at` for rotation policies. Sessions get `ip_address` and `user_agent` for security auditing. I'd also consider soft-delete with `deleted_at` — account recovery is cheaper than account recreation.
modelAnswer.senior: For production at scale: a `credential_history` table stores previous password hashes to prevent reuse (keep last 5-10). An `audit_log` captures every auth event (login, logout, failed attempt, password change) with IP, user-agent, and timestamp — essential for SOC2. An `account_links` table (provider, provider_user_id, user_id) prepares for social login without schema migration. For millions of users, the sharding key would be user_id. For GDPR deletion: anonymize the user record (null email, random name), hard-delete credentials and sessions, keep anonymized audit logs.

8.coachQuestion: What could go wrong with your authentication system? Think about failures, edge cases, and how someone could abuse it.

junior.point: Wrong credentials: generic error 'Invalid email or password' (never reveal which is wrong)
Brute force: rate limit login attempts (e.g. 5/min), lock account or add delay after N failures
SQL injection: use parameterized queries / ORM, never string concatenation
Timing attacks & user enumeration: run a dummy hash when user is not found so response latency is indistinguishable; use constant-time comparison (crypto.timingSafeEqual) for token verification

mid.point: Credential stuffing: attackers use leaked password lists; mitigate with rate limits + CAPTCHA
Account enumeration via registration ('email already taken') and password reset; use consistent responses
Session fixation: always regenerate session ID after successful login
CSRF protection for cookie-based sessions (SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies + anti-CSRF tokens)

Password strength per NIST SP 800-63B: minimum 8 characters (support 64+), ban composition/complexity rules (e.g. uppercase/symbol mandates) and periodic expiration; check against breached/compromised password lists

senior.point: Distributed brute force (IP rotation, botnet) — requires device fingerprinting, CAPTCHA, or IP reputation
Compromised credential checking (HaveIBeenPwned API integration at registration and password change)
Phishing awareness — magic link and reset email hygiene (no embedded password entry forms)
Incident response playbook for mass credential leaks (invalidation of sessions, forced reset)
Token theft via XSS — HttpOnly cookies, CSP headers, avoiding localStorage for sensitive tokens

modelAnswer.junior: Four main threats: (1) Wrong password — always return a generic error like 'Invalid email or password' without revealing whether the email exists. (2) Brute force — rate limit login to 5 attempts/minute and lock the account temporarily after 10 failures. (3) SQL injection — always use parameterized queries or an ORM, never concatenate input into SQL. (4) Timing attacks & user enumeration — password hashing takes 100-300ms. If an email doesn't exist, returning immediately reveals that fact via latency; always perform a dummy hash with equivalent work factor when the user isn't found so timing is uniform. Use constant-time comparison (e.g., crypto.timingSafeEqual) when checking tokens or signatures.
modelAnswer.mid: Beyond the basics: credential stuffing is the #1 real-world threat — attackers automate logins using leaked credentials from other sites. Mitigate with rate limiting + CAPTCHA after repeated failed attempts. Account enumeration also happens via the registration endpoint ('email already taken') — use a consistent response that doesn't reveal existence or send confirmation links regardless. Session fixation: always regenerate the session ID after successful authentication. CSRF: use SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies or anti-CSRF tokens. For password policies: NIST SP 800-63B mandates at least 8 characters (supporting up to 64+), explicitly discourages composition rules (demanding uppercase/special chars) and arbitrary periodic expiration, and instead recommends screening against known breached password lists.
modelAnswer.senior: At scale: distributed brute force uses botnets with rotating IPs — rate limiting per IP isn't enough. You need device fingerprinting, progressive CAPTCHA, and anomaly detection (unusual geography, impossible travel). Integrate HaveIBeenPwned's Pwned Passwords API to reject known-compromised passwords at registration and password change. For incident response: have a playbook for mass credential leaks — force password reset for affected accounts, invalidate all sessions, notify users, and update the audit log. Prevent token theft via XSS with HttpOnly cookies (can't be read by JavaScript) and strict Content-Security-Policy headers.

9.coachQuestion: What are the key trade-offs you'd evaluate when designing this authentication system? Pick at least two and explain the options.

junior.point: Sessions vs JWT: sessions are server-side (revocable, simple) vs JWT (stateless, cannot easily revoke without blocklist)
bcrypt vs argon2id: argon2id is memory-hard and GPU-resistant; bcrypt is widely supported and battle-tested
Cookie-based vs Authorization header: cookies are sent automatically by browsers (need CSRF protection) vs headers (manual handling in JS, vulnerable to XSS if in localStorage)

mid.point: Argon2 memory/time parameter tuning: balancing security (cost) vs server latency/throughput (~250ms target)
Session storage: database (simple, persistent) vs Redis (fast, memory-intensive, extra infrastructure)
Email verification UX: mandatory before login vs permissive with restricted permissions
Opaque random session tokens vs structured tokens with signed claims

senior.point: Horizontal scaling implications: sticky sessions vs shared cache (Redis) vs stateless JWT with short expiry
Multi-region session replication and consistency trade-offs (global vs regional latency)
Passwordless authentication as alternative (WebAuthn / Passkeys / magic links) vs password maintenance overhead
Cost and deliverability of transactional email infrastructure at scale
Token architecture for browser users (HttpOnly cookies) vs mobile / third-party API clients (Bearer tokens)

modelAnswer.junior: Two key trade-offs: (1) Sessions vs JWT — sessions store state on the server (easy to revoke, simple to implement, but need storage). JWTs are stateless (no server storage, but you can't easily revoke them — a compromised token is valid until expiry). For a single-user app, sessions are simpler and safer. (2) bcrypt vs argon2id — bcrypt is battle-tested and widely supported, but argon2id is specifically designed to resist GPU/ASIC attacks by requiring configurable memory. I'd choose argon2id for new projects.
modelAnswer.mid: I'd also evaluate: argon2 parameter tuning — more memory and iterations = more secure, but each login takes longer. Aim for ~250ms per hash. Session storage: a database is simplest (SQLite for us), Redis is faster but adds infrastructure. Email verification strategy: requiring verification before access is safer (prevents fake accounts) but increases friction — allowing limited access with a persistent 'verify your email' banner is a middle ground.
modelAnswer.senior: At scale: the session-vs-JWT choice has infrastructure implications. Sessions need a shared store for horizontal scaling (Redis cluster), sticky sessions (limits load balancing), or you accept that logout doesn't work cross-server. JWTs scale naturally but create a revocation problem (need a blocklist, which is essentially a session store). Consider passwordless auth (magic links or WebAuthn/passkeys) — better security, no password database to protect, but email deliverability becomes critical infrastructure.
